teile.einleitung: The **atlas** is the uppermost vertebra of the neck. It carries the head and joins it to the spine. Together with the second neck vertebra, it makes the many movements of the head possible.
wichtigste: The atlas is the first neck vertebra.
It is named after a Titan in Greek mythology.
Unlike most vertebrae, it has no vertebral body.
With the occipital bone, it forms the upper head joint, which mainly allows nodding.
The joint to the second neck vertebra, the axis, mainly allows turning the head.
The spinal cord runs through the large hole in the atlas.

abschnitte.text: The atlas is named after a **Titan in Greek mythology**. As a punishment, Atlas had to carry the vault of the sky on his shoulders. In a similar way, the first neck vertebra carries the **head**. So the name fits its job well.

Most vertebrae have a thick, round **vertebral body**. The atlas does not have one. It consists essentially of a front and a rear arch and looks like a **ring**. Through the large hole in the middle runs the **spinal cord**. At the sides, the atlas has strong parts with joint surfaces for the skull and for the second neck vertebra.

At the top, the atlas forms the **upper head joint** with the **occipital bone** of the skull. This joint mainly allows **nodding**, that is, the movement for “yes”. A slight tilting of the head to the side is also possible there.

The second neck vertebra is called the **axis**. It carries a peg-shaped projection, the **dens**, or tooth. This sticks up into the ring of the atlas and is held there by a strong **transverse ligament**. The atlas turns around this peg together with the head. The lower head joint between the atlas and axis mainly allows **turning the head** for “no”.

gewusst: In geography, too, a book of maps is called an atlas, also after the Titan of mythology.
Almost all mammals, even the giraffe, have seven neck vertebrae.

teile.einleitung: An anticoagulant is a medicine that slows blood clotting. Such drugs are often called “blood thinners”, although they do not really make the blood thinner. They are meant to stop dangerous blood clots from forming.
wichtigste: Anticoagulants slow blood clotting and prevent thromboses.
Heparin is named after the liver, from which it was first obtained.
Low-molecular-weight heparins are usually injected under the skin once a day.
In Switzerland, the vitamin K antagonist phenprocoumon has traditionally been used a lot.
Rivaroxaban blocks clotting factor Xa.
Protamine reverses the effect of heparin, and vitamin K that of the vitamin K antagonists.
Citrate or EDTA in test tubes bind calcium and so stop clotting.

abschnitte.text: When we hurt ourselves, the blood forms a **plug** that closes the wound. This is called **clotting**. Many proteins, the **clotting factors**, are involved in it. Sometimes, though, a clot forms inside a blood vessel, a **thrombosis**. If it comes loose, it can cause, for example, a pulmonary embolism or a stroke. An **anticoagulant** is meant to prevent this.

**Heparin** was first obtained from the **liver**, which is how it got its name: the Greek word for liver is “hepar”. Heparin has to be injected or given as a drip. Today **low-molecular-weight heparins** are often used. They are usually injected **under the skin once a day**, for example after an operation, to prevent thromboses. If the effect of heparin has to be reversed quickly, the antidote **protamine** is given.

To make several clotting factors, the liver needs **vitamin K**. **Vitamin K antagonists** disturb this process. In **Switzerland**, **phenprocoumon** has traditionally been used a lot, while in other countries **warfarin** is more common. Warfarin was originally developed from a substance that forms in **spoiled sweet clover**. Cattle that ate such clover suffered severe bleeding. **Vitamin K** is used as the antidote.

For some years there have been newer clotting inhibitors as tablets. They block a single clotting factor in a targeted way. **Rivaroxaban**, for example, blocks **factor Xa**. These drugs usually need to be checked in the laboratory less often. With all anticoagulants, however, there is a risk of **bleeding**, so they are dosed carefully.

Clotting inhibitors are also needed in the laboratory. Many **blood collection tubes** contain **citrate** or **EDTA**. These substances **bind calcium**. Without free calcium, blood cannot clot. In this way the blood sample stays liquid and can be examined.

gewusst: Warfarin was first used as a rat poison before it became a medicine.
The name warfarin comes from the Wisconsin Alumni Research Foundation, abbreviated WARF, which supported the research.

teile.einleitung: Bending means moving a joint so that the angle gets smaller. We are constantly bending arms, legs, fingers and back, when kneeling down, stooping or making a fist.
wichtigste: In a squat, you bend your knees and stand up again.
When kneeling down, you bend your leg at the knee.
Most of the finger flexors lie in the forearm.
The hamstring muscles bend the knee.
When lifting heavy things, you bend your knees to protect your back.
When stooping, the hip is bent.
The inside of the elbow is called the crook of the arm.

abschnitte.text: In **bending**, a joint is angled, and in **straightening** it is made straight again. For this there are special muscles, the **flexors** and the **extensors**. They work as **opposing partners**. In the upper arm, for example, the biceps bends the elbow. The **hamstring muscles** pull the lower leg backwards and so bend the **knee**.

For a **fist**, you roll all the fingers in and bend them. Most of the **finger flexors**, though, do not sit in the hand at all, but in the **forearm**. Long **tendons** run from there right into the fingers. You can feel this if you make a fist while holding your forearm. On the inside of the elbow lies the **crook of the arm**. When you bend your arm, a fold forms there.

In a **squat**, you go down with bent knees and straighten up again. This strengthens the leg muscles. When **kneeling down**, you angle the leg sharply at the knee. When lifting a heavy crate, you bend your **knees** and keep your back straight. In this way the strong leg muscles lift the load, and the **back** is spared.

If you stoop forwards to your toes, the upper body folds forwards at the **hip**. The hip joint is bent in doing so. In **Japan**, people often greet one another with a **bow**. In it you bend the upper body forwards. The deeper the bow, the more respect you show.

gewusst: The muscles that bend your fingers lie mostly in the forearm.
In Japan, the depth of a bow shows how much respect you have for someone.

teile.einleitung: The blood-brain barrier is a natural barrier between the blood and the brain. It protects the brain from harmful substances in the blood, but lets important nutrients through. In this way the surroundings of the delicate nerve cells stay stable.
wichtigste: The blood-brain barrier protects the brain from harmful substances in the blood.
It is formed mainly by the cells of the blood vessel walls in the brain.
These cells are especially tightly joined to one another.
Oxygen and glucose still get into the brain.
Many germs and toxins are held back.
For medicine it is a challenge, because many medicines also do not get through.
It was discovered through experiments with dyes between 1885 and 1913.

abschnitte.text: The **brain** is an especially sensitive organ that needs a very even environment. The **blood-brain barrier** therefore separates the bloodstream from the nerve tissue. It is not a wall that you can see, but a property of the fine blood vessels in the brain. You can imagine it as a strict doorman.

Blood vessels are lined on the inside with a layer of cells, the **endothelium**. In the brain, these cells are joined to one another almost without gaps by so-called **tight junctions**. In addition, star-shaped supporting cells, the astrocytes, wrap the vessels with their extensions. As a result, substances cannot simply slip through between the cells.

Small molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide pass easily through the barrier. For important nutrients such as **glucose** there are special transport proteins that bring them in in a targeted way. Fat-soluble substances such as alcohol or caffeine can also cross the barrier. Large molecules, many bacteria and some toxins, on the other hand, stay outside.

At the end of the 19th century, the German researcher Paul Ehrlich injected a dye into the blood of animals. Almost all organs were stained, only the brain was not. His pupil Edwin Goldmann later injected the dye directly into the fluid around the brain and spinal cord, and now only the brain was stained. From this people concluded that a barrier lies between blood and brain.

The barrier protects us, but makes the treatment of brain diseases difficult. Many medicines, for example some antibiotics, do not get into the brain. Researchers are therefore developing active substances that can overcome the barrier in a targeted way. In inflammations such as **meningitis**, the barrier can become more permeable.

begriffe.erklaerung: A barrier that controls which substances get from the blood into the brain.
The inner layer of cells of blood vessels.
Very tight connections between cells that let hardly anything through.
Star-shaped supporting cells in the brain.

gewusst: The brain makes up only about 2 per cent of body weight, but uses about 20 per cent of the energy.
At a few places in the brain the barrier is missing, so that the brain can monitor the contents of the blood.

teile.einleitung: The aorta is the largest blood vessel in the human body. It begins right at the heart and distributes oxygen-rich blood throughout the body.
wichtigste: The German name for the aorta is Hauptschlagader, meaning “main artery”.
Oxygen-rich blood flows in the aorta.
The first branches off are the coronary vessels, which supply the heart muscle.
The curved section above the heart is called the aortic arch.
The carotid arteries, among others, branch off from the aortic arch.
Below the diaphragm it is called the abdominal aorta.
At about the level of the belly button, it divides into the two iliac arteries.

abschnitte.text: The **aorta** begins at the **left ventricle**. Between the heart and the aorta lies the **aortic valve**, which, like a valve in a pipe, stops blood from flowing back. With every heartbeat, **oxygen-rich blood** is pumped into the aorta. Right at the start, the **coronary vessels** branch off. They supply the **heart muscle** itself with blood.

First the aorta climbs upwards for a short way. Then it curves backwards and to the left, forming the **aortic arch**. Large arteries branch off from it that supply the **head** and the **arms**. They include the **carotid arteries**, which bring blood to the brain. After that, the aorta runs down along the spine as the **thoracic aorta**.

The aorta passes through an opening in the **diaphragm**, the breathing muscle between the chest and the abdomen. Below it, it is called the **abdominal aorta**. Here arteries branch off to the stomach, intestines, liver and kidneys. At about the **level of the belly button**, the aorta divides into the two **iliac arteries**. These carry on to the legs.

As people get older, the wall of the aorta can become weaker. Then an abnormal, balloon-like widening can form, an **aortic aneurysm**. For a long time it often causes no symptoms. If it bursts, that is a life-threatening emergency. So a large aneurysm is often operated on beforehand, for example with an artificial vessel. Healthy blood pressure and not smoking protect the aorta.

gewusst: An adult’s aorta is about as thick as a thumb, with a diameter of around 2.5 to 3 centimetres.
The wall of the aorta is very elastic and stretches a little with every heartbeat.

teile.einleitung: The package leaflet is in every pack of medicine. It explains how to take the medicine correctly, when you must not take it and what side effects can occur.
wichtigste: The package leaflet is an instruction manual for a medicine.
In Switzerland it is officially called patient information.
For professionals there is a more detailed professional information.
“Very common” means: more than one in ten people treated.
“Rare” means: one to ten in ten thousand people.
The patient information has to be available in German, French and Italian.
If you have questions, the chemist’s or the doctor can help.

abschnitte.text: The **package leaflet**, in German “Beipackzettel” or “Packungsbeilage”, is in the pack of medicine. It explains what the medicine is for, how much you take and for how long. In Switzerland it is officially called **patient information**. The texts are checked by **Swissmedic**, the Swiss agency for therapeutic products. For doctors and pharmacies there is in addition a more detailed **professional information**.

With **side effects**, the frequencies are precisely defined. **Very common** means: more than one in ten people treated. **Common** means: one to ten in a hundred. **Uncommon** means one to ten in a thousand. **Rare** means one to ten in ten thousand, **very rare** even fewer. So most people notice nothing of rare side effects.

**Contraindications** are situations in which you must not take the medicine. One example is an **allergy** to the active substance. **Interactions** describe how medicines influence one another. Some strengthen or weaken each other. Food or alcohol can also change the effect.

In Switzerland the patient information has to be available in **German**, **French** and **Italian**. In this way people in all the large parts of the country can read it. That is why Swiss package leaflets are often long and closely printed. Anyone who does not understand something asks at the **chemist’s** or the doctor’s. This helps to avoid mistakes in taking the medicine.

gewusst: The words “common” and “rare” have a precisely defined meaning in the package leaflet.
Swiss package leaflets are often in three languages, so that they can be understood all over the country.

teile.einleitung: When you are ill or have hurt yourself, you go to the **doctor**. They examine the body, find out what is wrong and help you get well. There are many different kinds of doctors.
wichtigste: When someone is ill, a family usually goes first to the family doctor.
Paediatricians look after children in particular.
The dentist takes care of bad teeth.
With the stethoscope, the doctor listens to the heart and lungs.
At the surgery you wait in the waiting room.
In Switzerland, you show the insurance card of the health insurer.

abschnitte.text: The **family doctor** is usually the first place to go when you are ill. A **paediatrician** looks after babies, children and teenagers in particular. The **dentist** takes care of bad teeth. There are also specialists for the eyes, the skin, the heart and much more. If necessary, the family doctor sends you to such a specialist.

Usually you make an appointment beforehand. At the surgery, you report to the **medical receptionist** at the front desk. In Switzerland, you show your **insurance card** there so that the **health insurer** pays the costs. Then you wait in the **waiting room** until it is your turn. Often there are books and toys for children there.

First the doctor asks what hurts and since when. With the **stethoscope** she listens to the heart and lungs. With the **thermometer** you measure whether someone has a fever. To look into the throat, the doctor presses the tongue down with a **wooden spatula**. With a small lamp she looks into the ears.

At the end the doctor explains what is wrong and what helps. Sometimes rest, plenty to drink and sleep are enough. If you need a medicine, she writes a **prescription**, with which you get it at the pharmacy. At some visits you also get a **vaccination**. If you have questions, feel free to ask them.

gewusst: The stethoscope was invented in 1816 by the French doctor René Laennec.
In an emergency in Switzerland, you can reach the ambulance emergency number on 144.

teile.einleitung: The **eyebrows** are the arches of hair above the eyes. They protect the eyes and help us to show feelings. Every person normally has two of them.
wichtigste: The eyebrows lie above the eyes.
A person normally has two eyebrows.
They consist of short hairs.
They keep sweat away from the eyes.
When we are amazed, the eyebrows go up.
Eyebrows drawn down together often show anger.

abschnitte.text: The eyebrows lie **above the eyes**. They work like a small roof. When you sweat or it rains, they steer **sweat** and rainwater to the side. This way it does not run into the eyes. Sweat in the eyes stings and gets in the way of seeing.

The eyebrows are also important for our **facial expression**, that is, the movements of the face. When you are **amazed** or surprised, they go **up**. If they are **drawn down together**, the face often shows **anger** or that you are thinking hard. You can also tell sadness or worry from the eyebrows. In this way other people understand how we feel.

Eyebrows consist of **short hairs**. These grow much more slowly and stay shorter than the hair on the head. Usually the eyebrows are a **similar colour to the hair on the head**, sometimes a little darker. In old age they can turn grey or white, like the hair on the head.
Some people shape their eyebrows. With **tweezers** they pluck out single hairs. Others dye their eyebrows or draw them in with a pencil. Which shape is popular at any time changes with fashion.

gewusst: Researchers have shown that you recognise faces without eyebrows much worse.
A plucked eyebrow hair usually grows back after a few weeks.

teile.einleitung: Physical activity means that we actively use our body: when walking, playing, cycling or doing sport. Regular activity keeps the heart, muscles, bones and also the mind healthy. Experts recommend that children be active for at least an hour every day.
wichtigste: According to experts, children should be active for at least an hour every day.
Activity strengthens the heart, lungs, muscles and bones.
Walking to school is a healthy way to get there.
Before sport you should warm up.
After sport it is best to drink water.
Activity improves your mood and helps with learning.
Too much sitting in front of screens is unhealthy.

abschnitte.text: Our body has over 600 **muscles** that move the bones and joints. Physical activity is everything that makes these muscles work: running, climbing, dancing or climbing stairs. In it the body needs more energy, and the heart and breathing work faster. A distinction is made between everyday activity, such as walking and cycling, and deliberate **sport**.

Through activity, the heart becomes stronger and the lungs more efficient. Muscles and bones become stronger, which is especially important during growth. Activity helps to keep a healthy body weight. The body also releases substances that put you in a good mood, and you sleep better.

The World Health Organization and the Swiss Federal Office of Sport recommend that children and young people have at least **an hour** of activity a day. It is fine to get out of breath and break into a sweat. For adults, at least two and a half hours a week are recommended. Long periods of sitting should be interrupted regularly.

A simple way to more activity is the **way to school** on foot or by bike. Playing outdoors, stairs instead of the lift, or helping in the garden count too. In Switzerland hiking, cycling, swimming and, in winter, skiing are very popular. Many children take part in a sports club, for example in football, gymnastics or floorball.

Before sport you should **warm up**, for example with light running and hopping. This prepares muscles and joints for the load and avoids injuries. When sweating, the body loses water, which is why drinking is important. **Water** is best, and sweet drinks are mostly not needed.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tissue in the body that can contract and so make movement possible.
Light exercises before sport that prepare the body.
The ability to keep moving for a long time without quickly getting tired.
When someone moves too little, which harms health.

gewusst: When we laugh, numerous muscles in the face and belly are moved.
Switzerland has a network of hiking trails of over 65,000 kilometres, which is more than one and a half times round the Earth.

teile.einleitung: The biceps is the muscle at the front of your upper arm. When you “show your muscles”, you see it as a round bulge. It bends the arm and helps in turning the hand.
wichtigste: The biceps lies at the front of the upper arm.
It bends the arm at the elbow joint.
“Biceps” means “two-headed”, it starts with two heads at the shoulder.
When tensed, it becomes shorter and thicker.
It turns the palm upwards.
The biceps is a skeletal muscle that you move with your will.

abschnitte.text: The **biceps** lies at the front of the **upper arm**. Its name means “two-headed”, because “bi” means **two**. The muscle starts at the top with **two heads** at the shoulder. At the bottom it is fixed to the forearm by a tendon. That is why it can pull on the forearm.

When the biceps **contracts**, the arm bends at the **elbow**. In doing so the muscle becomes **shorter and thicker** and bulges like a little mountain. That is why children bend their arm and tense it when they show their “muscles”. The biceps works hard, for example, when you lift a **full bucket**. To straighten the arm, another muscle on the back is needed, the triceps.

The biceps can do even more. It turns the forearm so that the **palm faces upwards**. You need this, for example, when you hold soup on a spoon. It also helps when unscrewing something with the right hand. You can feel it yourself: put your hand on your upper arm and turn the other hand to and fro.

The biceps is a **skeletal muscle**. Such muscles you can control with your **will**. The brain sends a signal along the nerves, and the muscle tenses. It is different with the heart muscle, which beats by itself. Through training the biceps becomes stronger.

gewusst: The name biceps comes from Latin: “biceps” means two-headed.
There is also a biceps in the thigh, on the back of the leg.

teile.einleitung: The **respiratory rate** says how many breaths a person takes per minute. It depends on age, on effort and on the surroundings. It is controlled by the breathing centre in the brain.
wichtigste: The respiratory rate counts the breaths per minute.
A healthy newborn baby breathes about 40 times a minute at rest.
Adults breathe about 12 to 18 times a minute at rest.
The breathing centre in the brainstem controls breathing.
More carbon dioxide in the blood stimulates breathing most strongly.
Abnormally fast breathing is called tachypnoea.

abschnitte.text: A healthy **newborn baby** breathes about **40 times** a minute at rest. With age, breathing becomes slower. Adults breathe about **12 to 18 times** a minute at rest. With effort, fever or excitement, the respiratory rate rises, and in sleep it usually falls a little.

We do not have to think about breathing. The **breathing centre** in the **brainstem** controls it automatically. It constantly measures how much **carbon dioxide** is in the blood. If this value rises, breathing becomes faster and deeper. A rising carbon dioxide level is the strongest drive to breathe, stronger than a lack of oxygen.

abschnitte.titel: Measuring and calculating the respiratory rate
abschnitte.text: You count the breaths by watching how the chest or tummy rises. If you count 9 breaths in 30 seconds, you multiply by 2 and get a respiratory rate of **18 per minute**. From the rate and the amount of air, the **minute volume** can be worked out. If an adult breathes in 0.5 litres 15 times a minute, that is **7.5 litres** of air per minute.

Abnormally fast breathing is called **tachypnoea** in technical language, and slowed breathing **bradypnoea**. In **hyperventilation**, you breathe too fast and too deeply. In doing so you breathe out too much carbon dioxide. This can lead to tingling in the hands and around the mouth and to dizziness.

In the high mountains the air is thinner, because the air pressure is lower. Every breath therefore contains **less oxygen**. The body makes up for this by breathing faster and deeper. After a few days at altitude, the body gets used to it, for example by making more red blood cells.

gewusst: Together with pulse, blood pressure and temperature, the respiratory rate is one of the most important vital signs measured in hospital.
Breathing runs automatically, but you can also control it deliberately for a short time, for example when holding your breath.

teile.einleitung: Antigen presentation is the name for the process in which cells show small pieces of proteins on their surface. In this way the T cells of the immune system find out whether there is a germ or a diseased cell in the body. Without this process, the targeted defence could not start.
wichtigste: Antigens are substances that the immune system can recognise, often parts of germs.
What is presented are short pieces of protein, the peptides, on MHC molecules.
Dendritic cells are the most effective at activating naive T cells.
Proteins from the cytosol are broken up in the proteasome and brought into the endoplasmic reticulum through TAP.
To be activated, the T cell also needs a signal from B7 to CD28.
Without this extra signal, the T cell becomes unresponsive, or anergic.
In 2011 Ralph Steinman received the Nobel Prize for discovering dendritic cells.

abschnitte.text: Cells constantly show small pieces of protein, the **peptides**, on their surface. They are presented on special molecules, the **MHC molecules**. Almost all body cells carry **MHC class I molecules**. They show pieces of proteins from inside the cell. **MHC class II molecules** are carried mainly by specialised defence cells. They show pieces of substances that were taken in from outside.

Proteins from the **cytosol**, the fluid of the cell, are broken up in the **proteasome**. The proteasome is a kind of shredder of the cell. The transporter **TAP** then moves the peptides into the **endoplasmic reticulum**. There they are loaded onto MHC class I molecules and brought to the cell surface. If a cell is infected by a virus, it shows pieces of the virus in this way, and killer T cells can recognise it.

The **dendritic cells** are the most effective cells for activating **naive T cells** for the first time. They sit, for example, in the skin and in the mucous membranes. They take in antigens, for example by **macropinocytosis**, that is, through large folds of their membrane with which they swallow fluid together with dissolved substances. After that they **travel to the nearest lymph node**. Dendritic cells can even show foreign antigens that they have taken in on MHC class I molecules. This is called **cross-presentation**.

When a T cell recognises its antigen, that alone is not yet enough. It needs a second, **costimulatory signal**. This is supplied by the **B7 molecules** of the antigen-presenting cell. They bind to the receptor **CD28** on the T cell. If this signal is missing, the naive T cell becomes **unresponsive**, which is called **anergic**. This safeguard helps to stop the immune system from attacking the body itself.

The Canadian researcher **Ralph Steinman** discovered dendritic cells in the 1970s. In **2011** he received the **Nobel Prize** in Medicine for it. However, he had died a few days before the announcement, which the Nobel committee did not know. Normally the prize is not awarded after death, but in his case it was allowed to stand.

gewusst: Dendritic cells are named that way because their many projections remind us of the branches of a tree, “dendron” in Greek.
Without MHC molecules, T cells could not recognise germs inside cells at all.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who works or studies at a computer for a long time needs a well set up place. Screen, chair, desk and light should be arranged so that the back, neck and eyes are relieved. This is called ergonomics.
wichtigste: The top edge of the screen is at or just below eye level.
The screen stands about an arm’s length away, around 50 to 70 cm.
Your line of sight runs parallel to the window, so there is no glare and no reflection.
Your feet stand flat on the floor, your forearms lie roughly horizontal.
Regular short breaks with movement relieve the body.
In Switzerland, Suva gives recommendations for computer workstations.

abschnitte.text: The **top edge** of the screen is at or just below **eye level**. In this way you look slightly downwards, which spares the neck and eyes. The distance is about an **arm’s length**, so roughly 50 to 70 cm. With very large screens it can be greater. The screen stands straight in front of you so that you do not have to turn your head all the time.

The screen is best placed **to the side of the window**, so that your line of sight runs parallel to the window. Light from the front **dazzles**, and light from behind is **reflected** in the screen. Both strain the eyes. Curtains or blinds help in strong sun. Good room lighting is also important.

Your **feet** stand flat on the floor, and thigh and lower leg form roughly a right angle. If you cannot reach the floor, a **footrest** helps. When typing, your **forearms** lie roughly horizontal, and your elbows are at about a right angle. In this way shoulders and wrists stay relaxed. The height of the desk and the chair should match this.

When looking hard at the screen, you **blink** much less often. As a result the tear film is renewed less, and the eyes become **dry**. The **20-20-20 rule** helps: every 20 minutes you look for about 20 seconds at something about 20 feet, that is, about 6 metres, away. In this way the eye muscles relax.

Even the best workstation does not replace **movement**. Short breaks and changes of posture relieve the back, neck and eyes. It is best to stand up now and then and walk a few steps. In Switzerland the accident insurer **Suva** works for safety at work and health protection. Among other things it publishes checklists for computer workstations.

gewusst: The word ergonomics comes from Greek and means roughly “the study of work”.
Many office desks today can be adjusted in height, so that you can alternate between sitting and standing.

teile.einleitung: **Medicines**, also called drugs or medication, help against illnesses and pain. But they only work properly if you take them correctly. That is why there are clear rules about how to handle them.
wichtigste: A grown-up should always give children their medicines.
In Switzerland, you buy medicines at the pharmacy.
Every pack contains a patient information leaflet with important instructions.
For some medicines you need a prescription from the doctor.
Antibiotics help against bacteria, not against viruses.
Medicines belong out of children’s reach.

abschnitte.text: Medicines come in many forms. For swallowing, they are often a **tablet** or capsule, and for children also a syrup. There are ointments for the skin, drops for the eyes or nose, sprays and suppositories. Some medicines are also injected. Which form you need depends on the illness and on your age.

In Switzerland, you buy medicines mainly at the **pharmacy**. There, pharmacists advise on how to take a medicine correctly. For many medicines you need a **prescription**. The doctor writes it out so that you get exactly the right medicine. Simple remedies are also available without a prescription.

In every pack of medicine there is a slip of paper, the **patient information leaflet**. It says what the medicine is for, how much you may take and which **side effects** it can have. Children should never take medicines on their own. **A grown-up** should always give them and make sure the amount is right. Too much of a medicine can be dangerous.

**Antibiotics** are medicines against **bacteria**. Against viruses, for example in an ordinary cold, they do not help. Anyone who is given antibiotics should take them for as long as the doctor says. If antibiotics are used too often or wrongly, bacteria can become **resistant**. Then the drugs no longer work.

At home, medicines belong **out of children’s reach**, best of all in a locked cupboard. They should be kept dry and not too warm. On every pack there is an **expiry date**. If a medicine is out of date, you take it back to the **pharmacy**. There it is disposed of safely, so that it does not get into the environment.

gewusst: In Switzerland, the authority Swissmedic checks whether a medicine is approved.
The first antibiotic, penicillin, was discovered in 1928 by Alexander Fleming.

teile.einleitung: Bacteriophages, phages for short, are viruses that infect only bacteria. Their name means “bacteria eater”. They have made history in research and could become important in medicine again.
wichtigste: Bacteriophages are viruses that infect bacteria.
The Greek “phagein” means to eat or devour.
Félix d’Hérelle coined the term “bacteriophage” in 1917.
A phage’s genetic material sits in a protein shell, the capsid.
In the lytic cycle the bacterial cell bursts and releases new phages.
In the lysogenic cycle the phage DNA rests in the bacterium as a prophage.
In 1952 Hershey and Chase showed with the T2 phage that DNA is the genetic material.

abschnitte.text: The British researcher **Frederick Twort** observed as early as 1915 that something invisible can dissolve bacteria. The French-Canadian microbiologist **Félix d’Hérelle** described this more exactly in 1917 and coined the name **bacteriophage**. The Greek word “phagein” means to eat or devour. A bacteriophage is therefore, literally, a **bacteria eater**.

Phages are much smaller than bacteria. Their genetic material is surrounded by a protein shell, the **capsid**. It is made of many identical protein building blocks. In typical phages such as **T4**, the capsid sits as a head on a **tail** with fibres. With this the phage attaches itself to a bacterium and injects its genetic material into it.

In the **lytic cycle**, the phage forces the bacterium to make new phages at once. In the end the cell bursts and releases them. “Lysis” means dissolving. In the **lysogenic cycle**, the phage DNA is built into the bacterial chromosome. This **prophage** is copied along with it at every cell division. Only under stress can it become active again. Sometimes phages pick up pieces of bacterial DNA by mistake and pass them on. This is called **transduction**.

In 1952 **Alfred Hershey** and **Martha Chase** showed with the **T2 phage** that DNA is the genetic material. They labelled DNA and proteins differently, and only the DNA got into the bacteria. In **phage therapy**, phages are used against bacteria that cause disease. Well known for this is the **Eliava Institute** in Tbilisi, Georgia, founded in 1923. Because many bacteria are becoming insensitive to antibiotics, there is interest in it again in the West today.

gewusst: Bacteriophages are thought to be the most common biological entities on Earth.
Phages infect only bacteria and are harmless to humans.
In Georgia, phages have been used in medicine for almost a hundred years.

teile.einleitung: Blood pressure is the pressure with which the blood presses against the walls of the blood vessels. It arises because the heart pumps blood forcefully into the arteries. In a measurement you get two numbers, for example 120/80.
wichtigste: Blood pressure is the pressure of the blood in the arteries.
It is measured in millimetres of mercury, abbreviated mmHg.
The two numbers give the systolic and the diastolic pressure.
The upper value arises when the heart contracts.
The lower value arises when the heart relaxes.
A value around 120/80 counts as normal in adults.
Permanently high blood pressure can damage the heart, vessels and kidneys.

abschnitte.text: With every heartbeat, the heart pumps blood into the large **arteries**. In doing so the blood presses against the vessel walls, and this is **blood pressure**. It makes sure that blood reaches the smallest vessels in the toes and brain. Without enough pressure, the organs would not get enough oxygen.

The first, higher value is the **systolic pressure**. It is measured when the heart contracts and ejects blood. The second, lower value is the **diastolic pressure**, when the heart relaxes and fills with blood again. At 120/80, the upper value is therefore 120 and the lower 80 millimetres of mercury.

Blood pressure is usually measured with an inflatable **cuff** on the upper arm or wrist. The cuff briefly squeezes the artery shut and then slowly lets the air out. In the past the doctor listened for sounds with a stethoscope while doing this, today electronic devices often do it. It is best to measure at rest and sitting down.

If blood pressure is permanently too high, it is called **high blood pressure** or hypertension. It usually does not hurt, but can lead over the years to a heart attack, stroke or kidney damage. In Switzerland about one in four adults has high blood pressure. Too low blood pressure is mostly harmless, but can cause dizziness on standing up quickly.

Regular exercise, little salt and a healthy body weight help to keep blood pressure low. Not smoking and enough sleep are also important. With excitement or sport, blood pressure rises for a short time, which is normal. In children blood pressure is lower than in adults and rises with age.

begriffe.erklaerung: The upper blood pressure value, when the heart contracts.
The lower blood pressure value, when the heart relaxes.
Millimetres of mercury, the unit of measurement for blood pressure.
The technical word for permanently high blood pressure.

gewusst: The unit mmHg comes from old measuring devices in which a column of mercury was pushed up.
The giraffe has very high blood pressure, so that the blood gets up its long neck to the brain.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who is ill often needs bed rest. You stay in bed, take it easy and give the body time to get well. A few simple things make bed rest more pleasant.
wichtigste: Bed rest means staying in bed and resting.
In sleep the body can recover.
With a fever you do no sport.
A sick child with a fever stays at home.
Airing the room briefly brings fresh air into it.
A glass of water by the bed reminds you to drink.
Wet pyjamas are swapped for dry ones.

abschnitte.text: In **bed rest** you stay in bed and take it easy. In this way the body can gather strength. In **sleep** it saves an especially large amount of strength. It needs this to fight the illness. **Sport** is too strenuous for the body with a fever. Only when you are well again may you romp about and train again.

You usually speak of a **fever** from a body temperature of about 38 degrees. With a fever you need rest and stay **at home**. In this way you cannot infect others either, for example at school. Only when you are fit again do you go back. If the fever gets very high or you feel worse and worse, you call the doctor.

Fresh air does sick people good. So you **air** the room briefly more often and cover up warmly while doing so. Sick people should **drink** a lot. A glass of water or tea by the bed reminds you of this. Anyone who is sweating puts on **dry pyjamas**. Wet clothes cool the body down and are unpleasant.

In bed rest you should not exert yourself. Quiet activities are good, such as an **audiobook**, a book, drawing or quiet music. A puzzle on a tray also works well in bed. Playing on a screen for a long time, on the other hand, is tiring for the eyes and head. And anyone who is tired may simply sleep.

gewusst: A fever is really a protection: the body raises its temperature to fight germs better.
In sleep the body’s own defence works especially hard.

teile.einleitung: In **endurance training**, you train the ability to keep going for a long time in a targeted way. It mainly strengthens the cardiovascular system and the muscles. There are different methods, which you use depending on your goal.
wichtigste: Endurance training strengthens the cardiovascular system in particular.
Basic endurance is the foundation for almost all sports.
In the continuous method, you run for a long time without a break at an even pace.
In interval training, hard efforts and rests alternate.
People who train regularly often have a lower resting pulse.
The Cooper test lasts 12 minutes.

abschnitte.text: **Basic endurance** is the foundation for almost all sports. You build it up with **easy training**, that is, at a calm pace over a longer time. You can tell well whether the pace is right by whether you **can still talk**. If you go too fast, you get out of breath and soon have to stop. Typical sports for this are running, swimming, cycling and **cross-country skiing**.

In the **continuous method**, you run, swim or cycle for a long time **without a break** at an even, calm pace. In **interval training**, short, hard efforts alternate with **rests to recover**. For example, you run fast for a minute and then jog gently for two minutes. Many athletes combine both methods.

Besides the muscles, endurance training especially strengthens the **cardiovascular system**. The heart becomes stronger and pumps more blood with each beat. So it has to beat less often at rest: the **resting pulse falls** over months. In top athletes the heart can become clearly bigger and more powerful. This is called an **athlete’s heart**.

The **Cooper test** is used to check endurance. You run for **12 minutes** and try to cover as long a distance as possible. It was developed by the American doctor **Kenneth Cooper**. The distance run is compared with tables for the particular age and sex. The test is used in many schools and in the army.

gewusst: With his book “Aerobics”, Kenneth Cooper made endurance training known worldwide in the 1960s.
Just a few weeks of regular training noticeably improve endurance.

teile.einleitung: In blood pressure measurement, you determine the pressure in the arteries. You get an upper and a lower value. Anyone who measures properly and measures more than once gets reliable results.
wichtigste: The upper value is called systolic, the lower diastolic.
The abbreviation RR goes back to the Italian doctor Scipione Riva-Rocci.
With the stethoscope you hear the Korotkoff sounds.
The cuff should be at heart level.
Because blood pressure varies, if high blood pressure is suspected you measure on several days.
In long-term blood pressure measurement, a device measures for 24 hours.
In white coat hypertension, the value is raised only at the surgery.

abschnitte.text: When the **ventricles** contract, they press blood into the arteries. The pressure is then highest, and this is the **systolic** or upper value. In **diastole** the heart relaxes and fills with blood again. The pressure in the arteries falls to the **diastolic** or lower value. You write, for example, 120 over 80 mmHg.

The Italian doctor **Scipione Riva-Rocci** developed in **1896** a measuring device with an inflatable **arm cuff**. After his initials, professionals still often write blood pressure as **RR**. The Russian doctor **Nikolai Korotkoff** described in **1905** tapping sounds under the cuff. With these **Korotkoff sounds** you determine the upper and the lower value.

The cuff is pumped up so strongly that it squeezes the artery completely shut. Then no blood flows, and in the **stethoscope** it is silent. Now you let the air out slowly. When the pressure falls below the upper value, the blood forces its way through in spurts, and you hear a **tapping**. When the tapping disappears, the lower value has been reached. The cuff should be at **heart level**, otherwise the value is distorted.

Blood pressure **varies** with movement, stress, time of day and sleep. If **high blood pressure** is suspected, you therefore measure on several days. In **long-term blood pressure measurement**, you wear a cuff with a small device for 24 hours that also measures automatically at night. Some people are nervous at the doctor’s surgery, and their blood pressure rises there. This is called **white coat hypertension**, and at home the values are then normal.

gewusst: The name “white coat” comes from the white coats that doctors often wear.
As early as the 18th century, the Englishman Stephen Hales measured blood pressure in a horse with a long glass tube.

teile.einleitung: The abdominal muscles form a strong wall at the front and sides of the belly. They keep us upright, protect the organs and help with coughing, laughing and sitting up.
wichtigste: The abdominal muscles protect the organs in the belly.
Together with the back muscles, they hold the upper body upright.
The straight abdominal muscle runs at the front from the ribs to the pelvis.
The oblique abdominal muscles turn and tilt the upper body.
Trained abdominal muscles can look like a six-pack.
Sit-ups and the forearm plank train the abdominal muscles.

abschnitte.text: At the front of the belly there are no bones. There the **abdominal muscles** form a firm wall in front of the **stomach and gut** and protect them. Together with the **back muscles**, they hold the upper body like the two sides of a support. In this way you can sit and stand **upright**. If the abdominal muscles are weak, the back has to work more.

The **straight abdominal muscle** runs at the front from the ribs to the **pelvis**. It pulls the upper body forwards, for example when sitting up. Strips of **tendon** running across divide it into sections. In trained people this looks like a **six-pack**. At the sides lie the **oblique abdominal muscles**. They turn and tilt the upper body. Beneath them lies the **transverse abdominal muscle**, which wraps around the belly like a belt.

When you **cough**, the abdominal muscles push the air out of the lungs forcefully. That is why you feel the belly go hard. In **laughing** too, they contract again and again. After a long laugh they can therefore be tired and ache. They also tense when you sneeze or lift heavy things.

In **sit-ups** you lift your upper body up from lying down. The abdominal muscles do this work. In the **forearm plank**, you support yourself on your forearms and toes. The abdominal muscles then hold the body straight like a board. It is important to keep breathing calmly. It is good to train the belly and back equally.

gewusst: A six-pack arises because strips of tendon divide the straight abdominal muscle into separate sections.
Long laughing can give you real muscle ache in the belly.

teile.einleitung: The pancreas is an elongated gland in the upper abdomen that lies behind the stomach. It has two important jobs: it produces digestive juices and hormones such as insulin. In this way it helps with digestion and regulates blood sugar.
wichtigste: The pancreas lies behind the stomach in the upper abdomen.
Its technical name is pancreas; in German it is called “Bauchspeicheldrüse”.
It produces digestive enzymes and hormones such as insulin.
The pancreas is the organ that makes insulin.
Every day it releases about 1.5 litres of digestive juice into the small intestine.
Insulin lowers blood sugar, glucagon raises it.
In diabetes, insulin is lacking or does not work properly.

abschnitte.text: The pancreas lies across the upper abdomen behind the stomach. It is about 15 to 20 centimetres long and weighs around 70 to 100 grams. A distinction is made between head, body and tail. The head lies in a loop of the duodenum, and the tail reaches to the spleen.

The largest part of the pancreas makes the **pancreatic juice**. It contains **enzymes** that break down proteins, fats and carbohydrates from food. The juice flows through a duct into the duodenum, the start of the small intestine. It also neutralises the stomach acid in the food pulp.

In the pancreas lie tiny groups of cells, the **islets of Langerhans**. They make the hormones insulin and glucagon and release them directly into the blood. **Insulin** makes sure that sugar gets from the blood into the cells, and so lowers blood sugar. Glucagon works the other way round and raises blood sugar when it is too low.

If the pancreas makes too little insulin or none, blood sugar rises too far. This disease is called **diabetes mellitus**, or sugar disease. In type 1 diabetes, the immune system destroys the insulin-making cells, and those affected have to inject insulin. In the more common type 2 diabetes, insulin works less well, often encouraged by being overweight and too little exercise.

The islets of Langerhans are named after the German doctor Paul Langerhans, who described them in 1869. In 1921, Frederick Banting and Charles Best in Canada managed to obtain insulin. From 1922, people with diabetes were already being treated with it. This discovery saved the lives of countless people.

begriffe.erklaerung: The technical word for the Bauchspeicheldrüse.
A protein that breaks down or rebuilds substances, for example in digestion.
A hormone that lowers blood sugar.
Groups of cells in the pancreas that make hormones.

gewusst: The pancreas is a digestive gland and a hormone gland at the same time.
World Diabetes Day on 14 November recalls the birthday of Frederick Banting.

teile.einleitung: Almost every person has a belly button. It sits at the front in the middle of the belly and is really a small scar that you get as a baby.
wichtigste: The belly button lies at the front in the middle of the belly.
It is a small scar from baby days.
Bits of fluff from clothes sometimes collect in the belly button.
You clean it gently with water in the shower.
Mammals such as dogs have a navel too.
A particularly important place is called the “navel of the world”.

abschnitte.text: The **belly button** sits at the front of the belly, about in the middle. It is really a small **scar**. Every person gets it as a **baby**, in the first days after birth. After that the navel stays for a lifetime. In most people it curves inwards, and in some it bulges a little outwards.

Fine fibres come loose from clothes. They can collect in the belly button as little bits of **fluff**, especially with cotton clothes. It is best to clean the navel **gently with water** and a little soap in the shower. Afterwards you dry it well. You should not poke about in it with pointed objects.

**Mammals** such as dogs, cats or cows have a navel too. Often it is well hidden under the fur. Hens, frogs and fish, on the other hand, hatch from **eggs** and have no navel like this. So you can tell from the navel that an animal is a mammal.

abschnitte.titel: Behind the navel and in sayings
abschnitte.text: Behind the belly button lies the **gut** in many loops. It digests the food further. Above the belly comes the **chest** with the heart and lungs, then the neck. Because the navel lies in the middle, a particularly important place is also called the “**navel of the world**”. The ancient Greeks, for example, saw the place **Delphi** as the centre of the world.

gewusst: Many different kinds of bacteria live in the belly button, and most of them are harmless.
A navel shows that an animal is a mammal.

teile.einleitung: Sport is physical activity according to certain rules, alone or in a team, for fun or in competition. Anyone who is active for at least an hour a day stays fit and healthy. Sport trains not only the body, but also team spirit, endurance and concentration.
wichtigste: Children should be active for at least an hour every day to stay fit.
Sport trains endurance, strength, speed, flexibility and coordination.
Regular sport strengthens the heart, circulation and bones.
Before training you warm up, afterwards you recover.
In team sports you learn fair play and working together.
In Switzerland the Youth and Sport programme supports children and young people.
Enough sleep and recovery are part of training.

abschnitte.text: By **sport** we mean physical activities done by rules or with a goal. There are individual sports such as athletics or swimming and **team sports** such as football, handball or ice hockey. Some do sport for pleasure, others train for competitions. The biggest international competitions are the Olympic Games.

In sport, various abilities are trained: **endurance**, strength, speed and flexibility. To these is added **coordination**, that is, the skilful interplay of muscles and senses. Every sport demands these abilities to different degrees. A marathon runner needs a lot of endurance, a gymnast a lot of strength and flexibility.

With regular training the heart becomes bigger and stronger and pumps more blood with each beat. Muscles grow and the bones become firmer. The body learns to use oxygen better. The brain benefits too, because activity improves concentration and memory.

In Switzerland there are thousands of sports clubs in which many children and young people take part. The federal programme **Youth and Sport**, J+S for short, supports courses and camps for 5 to 20 year olds. Popular sports are football, skiing, swimming, floorball and gymnastics. Typically Swiss are also Swiss wrestling, called “Schwingen”, and “Hornussen”.

Before sport you should **warm up**, so that muscles and joints are ready. After training the body needs recovery, because it only becomes stronger in the break. Drinking plenty of water and eating a balanced diet provides the energy needed. Protective equipment such as a helmet, knee pads or shin pads helps to avoid injuries.

begriffe.erklaerung: The ability to keep up a load for a long time.
The good interplay of muscles, nerves and senses.
Fair behaviour in sport, that is, keeping to the rules and respecting your opponent.
The federal sports promotion programme for children and young people.

gewusst: The ancient Olympic Games already took place over 2,700 years ago in Olympia in Greece.
The International Olympic Committee has its seat in Lausanne, which is why Lausanne calls itself the “Olympic Capital”.

teile.einleitung: Basal cell carcinoma, also called basalioma, is a skin cancer. In people with fair skin it is the most common cancer of all. Fortunately it mostly grows slowly and can be treated well.
wichtigste: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common cancer in fair-skinned people.
It destroys tissue locally, but only very rarely forms metastases.
It occurs most often on the head and face.
The most important risk factor is the UV dose accumulated over a lifetime.
In most tumours, the Hedgehog signalling pathway is misregulated.
The standard treatment is surgical removal.

abschnitte.text: The risk of **basal cell carcinoma** rises with the **UV dose** that builds up over a whole lifetime. That is why it mainly affects older people and people who work a lot outdoors. Most tumours arise where a lot of sun has reached over decades: on the **head and face**, especially on the **nose**, **forehead** and **ears**.

A nodular basalioma is often a skin-coloured to reddish, **glassy shiny nodule**. Typical is a **pearly, beaded rim**. On the surface you often see fine, widened **little vessels**. Later a small sore can form in the middle that does not heal. Anyone who notices something like this should have a skin doctor look at it.

Basal cell carcinoma can destroy the surrounding tissue right down to the **bone**. **Metastases**, that is, secondary tumours, it forms only extremely rarely. That is why it is sometimes called **semi-malignant**, half malignant. In most tumours, genes such as **PTCH1** are altered. As a result the **Hedgehog signalling pathway** is permanently active. Medicines such as **vismodegib** block this pathway in advanced tumours.

Usually the tumour is **cut out** completely. Under the microscope it is checked whether the cut edges are clear. In **micrographically controlled surgery**, for example by Mohs’ method, the surgeon keeps cutting until the edges are free of tumour. In this way a lot of healthy skin is kept on the face. Protection is offered by **shade**, clothing, a hat and **sun cream**. In the mountains UV radiation is stronger, which is especially important in Switzerland.

gewusst: Basal cell carcinoma is common, but almost never forms secondary tumours.
With every metre of altitude UV radiation gets stronger, so you need especially good sun protection in the mountains.

teile.einleitung: So that we can look in all directions, **eye muscles** move the eyeball. Each eye has six outer eye muscles. They work fast and precisely, and mostly quite automatically.
wichtigste: Each eye has six outer eye muscles, which makes 12 in both eyes together.
The eye muscles are among the fastest muscles in the body.
Both eyes turn in the same direction at the same time.
When reading, the eyes move in small jumps.
The eyes also move in sleep, especially during dreaming.
Looking into the distance helps the eyes to recover.

abschnitte.text: An adult’s **eyeball** is almost a sphere and about **2.5 centimetres** across. It lies well protected in the eye socket of the skull. The **outer eye muscles** are attached to it. Each eye has **six** of them: four straight and two slanting muscles. In both eyes together that makes **12**.

When you look to the left, **both eyes turn to the left at the same time**. The brain controls the muscles of both eyes so that they work together. Only in this way do you see a single, clear picture. Unlike a **chameleon**, a human cannot turn their eyes **independently** in different directions.

The eye muscles are among the **fastest muscles** in the body. When **reading**, the eyes do not glide smoothly along the line. They move **in small jumps**, called saccades, and stop briefly in between. The **blink** is fast too: it lasts **less than half a second**.

The eyes also move **in sleep**, **especially during dreaming**. There is a phase of sleep with fast eye movements behind the closed lids. It is called **REM sleep**, after the English “rapid eye movement”. In this phase we dream especially vividly.

When reading or at a screen, the eyes look at something near for a long time. This strains the muscles in the eye. It helps to take a break regularly and **look into the distance**, for example out of the window. Blinking on purpose is also good for the eyes, because otherwise they can dry out.

gewusst: The eyes make a great many jumps every day without us noticing.
In someone with a squint, the two eyes do not look in exactly the same direction.

teile.einleitung: A base pair consists of two bases that face each other in DNA and hold together. Like the rungs of a ladder, they join the two strands of the double helix.
wichtigste: In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and guanine with cytosine.
An adenine-thymine pair has two hydrogen bonds, a guanine-cytosine pair three.
Adenine and guanine are purines, cytosine and thymine are pyrimidines.
Each base pair consists of one purine and one pyrimidine.
In RNA, uracil replaces thymine.
According to Chargaff’s rule, adenine and thymine occur equally often.
On heating above 90 degrees, the strands separate.

abschnitte.text: DNA is a **double helix**, a twisted ladder. The rungs are **base pairs**. There are four bases: **adenine** (A), **thymine** (T), **guanine** (G) and **cytosine** (C). A always pairs with T, G always with C. This is called **complementary base pairing**. A and T hold together with **two hydrogen bonds**, G and C with three. Stretches rich in AT are therefore easier to separate.

**Purines** have a double ring system. These include adenine and guanine. **Pyrimidines** such as cytosine and thymine have only one ring. Each base pair consists of a large purine and a small pyrimidine. So every pair is about the same length and the helix is **the same width everywhere**. **Erwin Chargaff** found out that in double-stranded DNA there is as much adenine as thymine and as much guanine as cytosine.

With Chargaff’s rule you can do sums. If a piece of DNA contains **20 per cent adenine**, then it also has 20 per cent thymine. The remaining 60 per cent is shared between guanine and cytosine, so **30 per cent** each. The two strands run in opposite directions. The opposite strand to 5'-ATGC-3' is therefore, also read from 5' to 3', **5'-GCAT-3'**.

In **RNA**, the base **uracil** occurs instead of thymine. It also pairs with adenine. When the genetic information is read, **guanine can also pair with uracil** at the third position of a codon. This is described by Francis Crick’s **wobble hypothesis**. If DNA is heated to above 90 degrees, the bonds break and the strands separate. This **denaturing** is used in **PCR**, a method for copying DNA many times over.

gewusst: A person’s genetic material consists of about three billion base pairs.
In 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick described the double helix of DNA.

teile.einleitung: A **booster vaccination** refreshes the protection of an earlier vaccination. It makes use of the memory of the immune system. As a result it works faster and more strongly than the first vaccination.
wichtigste: The primary vaccination builds up the first protection.
In a booster vaccination, memory cells are reactivated.
In the response to the booster, antibodies of the IgG class dominate.
Through affinity maturation, the antibodies bind better and better.
In Switzerland, a tetanus booster is recommended every 20 years for adults aged 25 to 65.
For tick-borne encephalitis, a booster is given every 10 years, while flu vaccination is repeated every year.

abschnitte.text: For many diseases you first get a series of vaccinations. This series is called the **primary vaccination** and builds up the first protection. Over time, the protection from some vaccinations fades. This is called **waning immunity**. A **booster vaccination** brings the protection back to a high level.

abschnitte.titel: The memory of the immune system
abschnitte.text: After the first vaccination, the immune system makes **memory cells**. They remember the germ. In the booster vaccination, they are **reactivated** and multiply quickly. This second reaction is called the **secondary response**. It is faster and stronger than the first. In it, antibodies of the **IgG** class dominate.

With repeated contact with an antigen, the antibodies get better. The defence cells change their blueprint slightly, and the cells with the best fitting antibodies win out. This process is called **affinity maturation**. In this way the antibodies bind ever more firmly to the germ.

The **Swiss vaccination schedule** is published by the Federal Office of Public Health and the Federal Commission for Vaccination. For adults **between 25 and 65 years old**, a booster against **tetanus** is recommended **every 20 years**, and more often after that. Against **tick-borne encephalitis**, which is passed on by ticks, a booster is given **every 10 years**.

The **flu vaccination** is a special case. Flu viruses constantly change their **surface proteins**. So the immune system no longer recognises new variants well. Every year a new vaccine is therefore made to match the viruses that are expected. So you are vaccinated anew every autumn.

gewusst: The English word “booster” means something that strengthens.
Whether a vaccination has to be refreshed depends on the germ and on the vaccine.

teile.einleitung: The antidiuretic hormone, ADH for short, controls how much water the kidneys keep in the body. “Antidiuretic” means that it slows down the passing of urine. In this way ADH helps to keep the body’s water balance steady.
wichtigste: ADH is made in the hypothalamus.
It is released into the blood in the posterior pituitary.
Another name for ADH is vasopressin.
It is a peptide hormone made of nine amino acids.
Mainly a rise in the osmolality of the blood plasma triggers its release.
Alcohol blocks the release of ADH, so you have to pass water more often.
If ADH is missing, central diabetes insipidus develops.

abschnitte.text: ADH is made by nerve cells in the **hypothalamus**, a small part of the diencephalon. Along long nerve fibres it reaches the **posterior pituitary**. There it is stored and, when needed, released into the blood. ADH is a **peptide hormone** and consists of only **nine amino acids**. Its second name is **vasopressin**, because in large amounts it also narrows the blood vessels.

The most important trigger is a **rise in the osmolality of the plasma**. That means that the blood has too many dissolved particles, such as salt, in proportion to the water. This happens, for example, when you have not drunk anything for a long time or have sweated a lot. Special sensor cells in the brain notice this. Then more ADH is released, and at the same time you feel thirsty. Heavy blood loss also leads to its release.

ADH works in the **collecting ducts** of the kidney. There it binds to the **V2 receptors** of the cells. The cells then build water channels, the **aquaporins**, into their wall. Through these channels, water is taken back from the urine into the blood. You then pass less urine, but it is darker and more concentrated.

**Alcohol blocks** the release of ADH. The kidneys then keep back less water, and you have to **pass water** more often. As a result the body loses fluid. This is one reason why alcohol can dry the body out.

If the body makes too little ADH, **central diabetes insipidus** develops. People with it pass very large amounts of pale, dilute urine, often several litres a day. They are constantly very thirsty. Despite the similar name, this disease has nothing to do with diabetes of the sugar kind. It is usually treated with an artificial substance that works in a similar way to ADH.

gewusst: “Diabetes insipidus” means roughly “tasteless flow”, because, unlike in sugar diabetes, the urine is not sweet.
In the morning the urine is often darker, because the body releases more ADH during the night.

teile.einleitung: Every day we breathe in **air** thousands of times. It is made up of several gases that you cannot see. Clean air to breathe is important for our health.
wichtigste: Air consists mainly of nitrogen and oxygen.
About one fifth of the air is oxygen.
Carbon dioxide is only a very small part of the air.
Even breathed-out air still contains quite a lot of oxygen.
Exhaust fumes pollute the air in cities.
Cigarette smoke harms the lungs.

abschnitte.text: Air is a mixture of gases. About four fifths is **nitrogen**, and about **one fifth is oxygen**. There are also small amounts of argon and only a very little **carbon dioxide**. There is also water vapour in the air. You cannot see air, but you can feel it when it moves: outdoors you notice this as **wind**.

When you breathe in, the lungs take **oxygen** from the air. The blood carries it to all the cells in the body. When you breathe out, we give off **carbon dioxide**. But in the air we breathe out there is still **quite a lot of oxygen**. That is why rescue breaths work in first aid.

If many people are in a closed room for a long time, the air becomes **stuffy**. It then contains more carbon dioxide and moisture. Then it helps to **open the window** and air the room well for a short time. In winter, the air indoors is often very dry. A **humidifier** makes the air moister.

In cities, the air is polluted mainly by **exhaust fumes** from cars, heating systems and factories. This also includes fine dust, **particulate matter**. In the **forest** the air is usually cleaner, because trees filter dust out of the air. **Cigarette smoke** is especially harmful. It harms the lungs, even in people who only breathe in the smoke from others.

gewusst: An adult breathes in many thousands of litres of air in one day.
In Switzerland, many stations constantly measure how clean the air is.

teile.einleitung: Molars sit at the back of the mouth and are the strongest chewing tools we have. They grind up food so that we can swallow and digest it well.
wichtigste: The molars stand at the back on the left and right of the mouth.
They grind food like a mill.
Their chewing surface is broad and has cusps and grooves.
Another word for molar is grinding tooth, and the technical term is molar.
At about 6 years old the first big permanent molar comes.
The very last molars are called wisdom teeth.

abschnitte.text: The **molars** stand at the back on the left and right of the mouth, near the cheeks. In German they are called “Backenzähne”, or cheek teeth, for this reason. At the front of the mouth the incisors cut, and the canines hold things fast. The molars are broad and strong. With them you chew a hard **nut** into small pieces.

The **chewing surface** of a molar is broad and has **cusps** and small **grooves**. Top and bottom, the teeth fit into each other. In this way the food is ground fine, as in a mill. That is why they are also called **grinding teeth**. The technical term is **molar**, from the Latin word for millstone.

At about **6 years old**, the first big permanent molar grows behind the milk teeth. It is also called the **six-year molar**. No milk tooth falls out for it, it simply comes in addition. More molars follow later. The very last ones are the **wisdom teeth**. They often come only at 17 or later, and sometimes not at all.

Bits of food easily stick in the **grooves** of the chewing surface. There, bacteria can cause **tooth decay**, that is, holes in the tooth. That is why you have to clean the molars especially thoroughly. Dentists can **seal** the grooves with a thin protective varnish. In many Swiss municipalities there is a **school dental service** that regularly checks children’s teeth.

gewusst: Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the whole human body.
The first permanent molar comes without a milk tooth falling out for it.
Some people never get wisdom teeth.

teile.einleitung: Blind people can see little or nothing at all. With aids such as the white cane, Braille and screen readers, they manage their everyday life. Hearing and the sense of touch play a big part in this.
wichtigste: Braille, the writing made of dots, was invented by Louis Braille of France.
One character has at most six dots in two columns.
The white cane shows others that someone is blind.
In Switzerland, white guide lines with grooves on the ground help.
Screen readers read out texts on the computer.
On many medicine packs the name is given in Braille.

abschnitte.text: **Louis Braille** was born in **France** in 1809. He went blind as a small boy. At about **15 years old** he developed a writing of raised **dots** that is named after him. One character consists of at most **six dots** in two columns. Depending on which dots are raised, a different letter results. You read the writing with your fingertips.

The **white cane** shows other people that someone is blind. With it you feel the way ahead. In Switzerland, on pavements and in stations there are **white guide lines** with **grooves** on the ground. You feel them with the cane or your feet. They lead, for example, to platforms or pedestrian crossings.

Blind people pay close attention to **sounds** and feel their surroundings. In this way they replace part of seeing. From the sound they can tell, for example, whether a room is big or small. Smell also helps with orientation. Some also have a guide dog.

A **screen reader** reads out text on the screen with a computer voice. Some devices also show the text in Braille on a **Braille display**. On many **medicine packs** the name is given in Braille. In this way blind people can tell them apart. Phones too can be operated by voice.

gewusst: Braille developed his writing from a night writing of dots and dashes that was meant for soldiers.
On some banknotes and lift buttons there are tactile marks for blind people.

teile.einleitung: **Bronchial asthma** is a long-lasting inflammation of the airways. In an attack, the bronchi narrow and breathing becomes hard. Asthma is not infectious and can now usually be treated well.
wichtigste: Asthma is a chronic inflammation of the airways.
In an attack, the airways narrow.
A wheezing sound when breathing out is typical.
Pollen, animal hair or dust can trigger an attack.
A reliever inhaler quickly widens the bronchi.
Asthma is not infectious, and children whose asthma is well treated can usually do sport.

abschnitte.text: Air reaches the lungs by way of the windpipe and the **bronchi**. In asthma, these airways are permanently slightly inflamed and react very sensitively. In an attack, the muscles around the bronchi tighten, the lining swells and sticky mucus forms. The airways **narrow**, and breathing out in particular becomes hard.

In **allergic asthma**, for example, **flower pollen**, animal hair or house dust mites set off an attack. Cold air, smoke, infections or heavy exertion can also cause symptoms. Typical are coughing, difficulty breathing, a feeling of tightness in the chest and a **wheeze** when breathing out. Asthma is **not infectious**.

Many people with asthma take a medicine every day that dampens the **inflammation**, often as a spray to inhale. In an attack, a **reliever inhaler** helps, which quickly widens the bronchi. An inhaling aid, the so-called **spacer**, is a tube between the inhaler and the mouth. With it, more of the drug reaches the lungs and less stays behind in the mouth.

With a **peak flow meter** you measure how fast you can breathe out at most. If the value falls, the airways are narrower than usual. In this way you can notice early when the asthma is getting worse. Asthma differs from the lung disease **COPD** mainly in that the narrowing of the airways is largely **reversible**.

A child whose asthma is well treated can usually **do sport without problems**. It is important to warm up well and to have the reliever inhaler with you. Teachers and coaches should know what to do in an attack. Many top athletes have asthma and still win medals.

gewusst: Asthma is one of the most common chronic illnesses in children.
The word asthma comes from Greek and means panting or hard breathing.

teile.einleitung: Before sport you do a **warm-up**. In it you prepare the body for the effort. The muscles, heart and joints slowly get going, and you are less likely to hurt yourself.
wichtigste: In a warm-up the muscles become warm and loose.
The pulse rises slowly as you do it.
In school sport, the warm-up lasts about 10 minutes.
Gentle running and hopping are good exercises for warming up.
With arm circles you loosen the shoulders.
After training comes the cool-down.

abschnitte.text: In a warm-up the **muscles** become warm and loose. They can then contract and stretch better. The **joints** also become more mobile. The mind also gets ready for the sport. Anyone who warms up well can do more and is **less likely to hurt themselves**, for example with a pulled muscle.

In a warm-up the **pulse rises slowly**. The heart pumps more blood, and breathing becomes faster. In this way the muscles get more oxygen. Body temperature rises slightly. It is important not to start at full strength straight away, but to increase the effort bit by bit.

**Gentle running and hopping** are good for warming up. In **jumping jacks**, you jump and clap your hands together above your head while your legs move apart. With **arm circles** you loosen the shoulders. High knees, skipping and little games of tag are also good. In school sport, the warm-up usually lasts **about 10 minutes**.

After training it is best not to stop at once. In a **cool-down**, you jog slowly for a few more minutes. In this way the heart and breathing calm down bit by bit. After that you can stretch the muscles gently and drink enough.

gewusst: Professional sportspeople also warm up thoroughly before every match or race.
In cold weather, the warm-up is best a little longer.

teile.einleitung: The apple is the most popular fruit in Switzerland. It is crisp, juicy and full of vitamins. Apples grow on trees and are harvested mainly in autumn.
wichtigste: The apple is the most popular fruit in Switzerland.
Many vitamins are in and just under the skin.
Before eating an apple with its skin, you should wash it.
A cut apple turns brown because it reacts with the air.
Thurgau is jokingly called “Mostindien” because of its many apple trees.
Süssmost is fresh apple juice.
Most apples are harvested in autumn.

abschnitte.text: Apples contain a lot of **water**, fruit sugar, vitamins and **fibre**. Especially many vitamins are **in and just under the skin**. So it is worth eating the apple with its skin. But first you should **wash** it well, so that dirt and residues come off. An English saying goes: **“An apple a day keeps the doctor away”**.

In Switzerland, the **apple** is the **most popular fruit**. Many apples grow in eastern Switzerland. The canton of **Thurgau** has so many apple trees that it is jokingly called **“Mostindien”**, roughly “Cider India”. Most apples are harvested in **autumn**. Stored well in cool rooms, however, Swiss apples can be bought almost all year round. Well-known varieties are, for example, Gala, Golden Delicious, Braeburn and Boskoop.

Juice is pressed from apples. Fresh apple juice is called **Süssmost** in Switzerland. If you let the juice ferment, you get **Most**, also called cider, which contains alcohol. Apples are also used to make apple sauce, dried fruit or cakes such as the popular apple tart, the “Apfelwähe”.

If you cut an apple open, the cut surface turns **brown** after a short time. This is because substances in the flesh **react with the oxygen in the air**. A particular enzyme in the apple speeds this process up. The brown apple is still perfectly good to eat. A few drops of **lemon juice** slow the browning.

gewusst: Worldwide there are thousands of different apple varieties.
Apples float on water because they contain a lot of air in the flesh.

teile.einleitung: In appendicitis, usually the appendix is inflamed, a small attachment on the caecum. Typical are stomach pains at the lower right. Often the appendix has to be removed in an operation.
wichtigste: Usually it is not the caecum itself but the appendix that is inflamed.
The caecum is the start of the large intestine, at the lower right of the belly.
Typical are pains at the lower right, often with feeling sick and fever.
Often the appendix is operated out.
With bad stomach pains, you go quickly to the doctor.

abschnitte.text: The **caecum**, in German “Blinddarm”, is the start of the **large intestine**. It lies at the lower right of the belly, where the small intestine opens into the large intestine. From it hangs a small, narrow tube, the **appendix**. When people speak of “Blinddarmentzündung”, it is usually really the appendix that is inflamed. The technical term for this is **appendicitis**.

It often begins with stomach ache around the navel. Later the pain usually moves to the **lower right**. Often **feeling sick**, vomiting, little hunger and a mild **fever** come with it. Walking, coughing or hopping can make the pain worse. With such symptoms you go quickly to the doctor, because an inflamed appendix can burst.

Often the inflamed appendix is removed in an **operation**. Nowadays this is often done with **keyhole surgery** through small cuts. People can live well without an appendix. After a few days you can usually go home. Sometimes mild cases are also treated with medicines against bacteria.

gewusst: Appendicitis is one of the most common reasons for an abdominal operation in children and young people.
The appendix contains a lot of defence tissue and probably helps the immune system in the gut.
